Wimp
WIMP
noun (Gen X slang)
Origin uncertain; perhaps from whimper, and J. Wellington Wimpy, the soft-spoken, hamburger-loving character of E. C. Segar’s Popeye comic strip (from 1931), is often suggested as an influence. American slang by the 1960s for a feeble, timid, ineffectual man; Gen X used wimp and wimp out (to quit from fear) as playground staples of the 1980s, and in 1987 Newsweek applied "the wimp factor" to Vice President George H. W. Bush. Derived wimpy.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A wimp is a man without backbone: he cannot make a decision, will not stand up for anyone, and folds the moment someone pushes. Gen X boys used it on each other in the gym, and in 1987 the national press used it on a vice president. The Christian observation is that Scripture expects strength from men and defines it carefully. David’s charge to Solomon was plain: "be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man" (1Ki 2:2). Joab rallied the army: "Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God" (2Sa 10:12). Paul’s word to the church: "be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might" (Eph 6:10). But the world often mistakes meekness for wimpiness, and Scripture will not allow that confusion. Christ said, "I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mat 11:29) — and the same Jesus made a scourge of cords and drove the money changers from the temple. Meekness is strength under control, not the absence of strength. "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). The real wimp, in God’s eyes, is not the gentle man but the man who will not lead, will not protect, and will not speak up for the truth because it might cost him. A father can teach his son to be strong in the Lord, gentle with the weak, and immovable where God has spoken — the kind of man the world has never managed to call a wimp.

Webster 1828 Definition

American slang (1960s, origin uncertain) for a feeble, timid man, a Gen X playground staple; Scripture commands, shew thyself a man (1Ki 2:2), and shows in Christ that meekness is strength under control (Mat 11:29).

WIMP, n. (Gen X slang, 1960s origin, 1980s peak, United States) A feeble, timid, or ineffectual person, especially a man. "Don’t be a wimp — tell the coach what happened."

Derived wimpy, adj.; wimp out, v., to back down from fear. Origin uncertain; perhaps whimper; Popeye’s J. Wellington Wimpy (1931) often suggested.

1987: Newsweek’s "wimp factor" cover on George H. W. Bush carries the word into politics.

No entry in Webster 1828; the word is 20th-century American slang of uncertain origin.

Decode for parents: do not let your son confuse meekness with weakness; teach him strength that leads, protects, and rules its own spirit.

Key Scripture

1Ki 2:2 — "I go the way of all the earth: be thou strong therefore, and shew thyself a man;"

2Sa 10:12 — "Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the LORD do that which seemeth him good."

Eph 6:10 — "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might."

Mat 11:29 — "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

Pro 16:32 — "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city."

Modern Corruption

Wimp mocks weakness and often mistakes gentleness for it; Scripture calls men to be strong in the Lord and shows in Christ that meekness is strength under rule.

expand to see more

The confusion of meek and weak. The Gen X culture that coined wimp also tended to treat any gentle man as one. Scripture separates the two. Christ was meek and lowly (Mat 11:29), yet He overturned tables in the temple and set His face toward Jerusalem. He who rules his spirit is better than he who takes a city (Pro 16:32). A man who can hold his temper and his tongue has more strength, not less.

The real wimp. Scripture’s weak man is the passive man: Adam silent beside his wife, Eli who would not restrain his sons, Pilate washing his hands. The charge to Solomon, "shew thyself a man" (1Ki 2:2), was a charge to keep God’s law and lead. Fathers today face the same call: to play the men for our people (2Sa 10:12), strong not in themselves but in the Lord and in the power of His might (Eph 6:10).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Origin uncertain (perhaps whimper; Popeye’s Wimpy, 1931) → 1960s American wimp → 1980s wimp out → 1987 "wimp factor"; Scripture: be strong in the Lord (Eph 6:10); meek and lowly (Mat 11:29).
